title: Observability in System Design
summary: Logs, metrics, and traces answer different questions about a running system — knowing which one to reach for is what separates observability from a wall of dashboards.

slides.markdown:
**Observability** means you can answer "why is this broken?" using data you already collect, instead of adding print statements after the fact. It rests on three pillars — **logs** (discrete events), **metrics** (numbers aggregated over time), and **traces** (one request's path across services) — and each answers a different question.

A green dashboard tells you the average is fine; it says nothing about the one customer whose checkout just failed. This topic covers what each pillar actually answers and why "we have logs" isn't the same as "we're observable."

slides.sectionTitle: Why "is it working?" needs more than a green dashboard
slides.markdown:
A dashboard showing 99.9% uptime and a low average latency can still hide a system that's badly broken for real users. Averages smear over outliers: if 1% of requests take 30 seconds while the rest take 50ms, the average still looks fine — but that 1% might be every user paying with a specific card type, every single time.

**Observability** is the property that lets you ask a *new* question about your system's behavior without shipping new code first, not just check the handful of questions you thought to graph in advance. A dashboard is a fixed set of pre-answered questions; observability is the ability to ask one you didn't anticipate.

Interview signal: don't just say "we'd monitor it" — say what you'd be able to ask *after* something breaks that you can't ask today.

slides.sectionTitle: The three pillars: logs, metrics, and traces — what each answers
slides.markdown:
**Logs** are timestamped, discrete events — "user 8821 checkout failed: card declined." They answer *what exactly happened*, with full detail, for one event at a time.

**Metrics** are numbers aggregated over time — request count, p99 latency, error rate per minute. They answer *how is the system doing overall*, cheaply, at any timescale, but they throw away per-request detail to get there.

**Traces** follow one request as it hops across services — API gateway to auth to payments to inventory — recording how long each hop took. They answer *where in this specific request did the time go*.

None of the three substitutes for the others: a metric tells you latency spiked, a trace tells you which service caused it, and a log tells you the exact error that service hit.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: the same incident seen through logs, metrics, and traces
slides.markdown:
![One incident viewed as a metric, a trace, and a log](assets/three-pillars-incident.svg)

The same 14:02 incident looks different in each view. The metric shows *that* something broke and roughly *when*. The trace narrows it to *which service* — payments, not auth or inventory. The log gives the *exact reason* — a gateway timeout, not a bad request.

Working top-down (metric → trace → log) is usually the fastest path from alert to root cause.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: logs vs metrics vs traces on cost, granularity, and use case
slides.markdown:
| | Logs | Metrics | Traces |
|---|---|---|---|
| Granularity | Per-event, full detail | Aggregated, detail lost | Per-request, cross-service |
| Storage cost | High — every event, raw text | Low — pre-aggregated numbers | Medium-high, especially at 100% sampling |
| Best question | "What exactly happened?" | "Is the system healthy right now?" | "Where did this one request's time go?" |
| Typical retention | Days to weeks | Months (already compact) | Days, often sampled |

**How to decide:** reach for metrics first (cheap, always-on, good for alerting), traces when you need to localize a slow or failing request across services, and logs when you need the exact detail neither of the other two captures.

slides.sectionTitle: Where observability fits in the design conversation, not just ops
slides.markdown:
Observability is often treated as an ops afterthought — something added once a service is in production and something has already gone wrong. In a system-design interview, that's a missed signal: naming what you'd measure and how you'd correlate it across services shows you're designing for the system's entire lifecycle, not just its happy path.

Concretely, this means naming your **golden signals** (latency, traffic, errors, saturation — covered later in this group) and a way to correlate a single request across the services you just drew, while you're still sketching the architecture, not after.

An interviewer who asks "how would you know this is broken?" is testing whether observability was ever part of your design thinking at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: having logs but no way to correlate them across services
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Every service logs its own errors, so we can debug anything."

**Why it's wrong:** a single user request in a microservices architecture might touch six services. If each service's logs carry no shared identifier, debugging one failed request means manually guessing which lines in six separate log streams, at roughly the same timestamp, belong to the same request — a process that gets impossible fast under real traffic volume.

**Correct model:** every request needs a **correlation ID** generated at the edge and threaded through every downstream call and every log line, so "show me everything about this one request" is a single query, not an investigation. This is the seed of distributed tracing, covered next in this group.

slides.sectionTitle: Monitoring vs observability: knowing what to watch for vs being able to ask anything
slides.markdown:
**Monitoring** is watching a predefined set of signals for known failure modes — a dashboard for CPU, a dashboard for error rate, an alert if disk usage crosses 90%. It answers questions you thought to ask in advance, and it's necessary, but it has a ceiling: it can only tell you about the failure modes someone anticipated and built a check for.

**Observability** is the broader property of being able to ask a genuinely new question about the system's internal state, using existing data, without shipping new instrumentation first — "which of our 200 customers on the new pricing tier are seeing elevated latency, and does it correlate with which database shard they're on?" is not a question any dashboard was built for in advance, but a system with rich enough logs, metrics, and traces can still answer it by querying and correlating the data that's already there.

The practical distinction: monitoring catches the failure modes you predicted; observability is what lets you debug the ones you didn't. Both matter, but conflating them, thinking a wall of dashboards means you're observable, is the mistake this topic is really warning against.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: using all three pillars together to find a root cause
slides.markdown:
An alert fires: checkout p99 latency crossed 3 seconds, up from a normal 400ms. The **metric** told you something is wrong and roughly when it started, but nothing about why — at this point you don't yet know if it's one service, one region, or one dependency.

Opening a handful of slow **traces** from that time window shows a pattern: every slow trace has one span in common, a call from the checkout service to the inventory service, consistently taking 2.5+ seconds while every other span in the same traces looks normal. That narrows the search from "the whole system" to one specific service boundary.

Pulling **logs** from the inventory service for that time window, filtered to the slow requests' correlation IDs, shows the actual reason: a burst of `connection pool exhausted, waited 2400ms for a free connection` errors, pointing at a database connection pool sized too small for the current load. The metric found the incident, the trace localized it to one hop, and the log gave the exact, actionable cause — each pillar did the part of the job the other two couldn't, and skipping any one of them would have left a real gap in the investigation.
